brief.head: Andheri to Arkansas
brief.text: A sale from Andheri to Bandra troubles nobody, Amit Varma said. Why should it matter if the buyer sits in Arkansas? Every trade is two individuals both gaining. {018-C09}

brief.head: South of the Vindhyas
brief.text: Warming will hit hardest above the Vindhyas, Ajay Shah said. Families should be able to sell up and move south, but frozen land markets keep them hugging the land. {018-C12}

brief.head: Spare the middleman
brief.text: Anger at middlemen is easy populism, Ajay Shah warned. Traders working within the state’s rules are not the villains: “all that’s going on here is a lack of freedom.” {018-C16}

brief.head: Harder than code
brief.text: Ajay Shah would neither ban gene editing nor rush it. Editing DNA, he said, is “a wee bit harder than editing computer code”, and code goes wrong. {018-C17}

brief.head: The choke point
brief.text: India’s farm controls came from an earlier generation’s agricultural economics, Ajay Shah said. “What is wrong in India is the lack of ideas, is the lack of knowledge.” {018-C18}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on what ails Indian farming
lead.head: The state is the pest
body: Tomatoes in India had lately swung between 200 rupees a kilo and two rupees, Ajay Shah said. People flying in from abroad were asked to fill the rest of their bags with them. {018-R05}

For Shah and Amit Varma, the tomato was a way into a larger question: what is wrong with Indian agriculture? One problem at a time, they kept arriving at the same answer. The state is at the heart of it, and farmers are denied freedoms city people take for granted.
## Prices that ration

Shah began with how prices work. If 90 units of tomatoes reach the market instead of 100, the price has to rise until enough buyers walk away. “So the price system should be understood as a rationing mechanism,” he said. {018-C01}
Staples such as wheat and rice, bought without a glance at the price, need huge swings to close a small gap. Avocados, a luxury, need only a small rise.

Paul Samuelson’s cobweb model adds the boom and bust: a high price makes everyone plant, and the glut crashes the price. But the model needs farmers to sow by looking backward, inputs that are fixed and no way to store food, Shah said.
A swing from two rupees to 200, he said, is peculiar to India. Elsewhere, futures markets, storage, domestic trade and international trade keep food markets calm.
## Penned in by law

India has hobbled every one of those four. Farmers must sell at their local Agricultural Produce Market Committee, a state-made monopsony. In one old study Varma recalled, farmers got two rupees for tomatoes that consumers bought for twenty. {018-C06}
Trade bans keep farmers below world prices, which the farmer leader Sharad Joshi called a negative subsidy. City slickers think farmers live off handouts. In net terms, Varma said, they are paying.
Holdings of one or two acres are “fundamentally subscale”, Shah said, and they breed near-feudal dependence on one local lender and buyer.
Land law locks the trap. Farmland can be sold only to another farmer, for farming, so its price stays low and its owners can neither exit nor borrow against it.
In 1991 the rest of the economy was liberalised and agriculture was not, Varma said. Between 50 and 60 per cent of Indians are estimated to depend on farming, which produces 14 per cent of GDP.

Minimum support prices bent what India grows. When cereals got them, farmers left pulses, the main protein for those who do not eat animals, and the state ended up feeding the diabetes epidemic. {018-C14}
## The farmers who fought back
Varma’s hero was Joshi, who came home in 1977 from work in Bern and with the UN, bought a farm near Pune and built the Shetkari Sanghatana. Lakhs came to its rallies.
In 2002, bollworms wrecked cotton across Gujarat, except on farms that had planted banned BT cotton bought on the black market. The government ordered the surviving crop destroyed.
Joshi’s farmers stood on the fields and said “over our dead bodies”. The ban was lifted, and in time, Varma said, over 90 per cent of India’s cotton was BT. {#ninety}
“It was farmers who decided even if the government has banned it, we have to save ourselves,” Varma said.
Joshi later spent years in the Rajya Sabha, where, Varma said, nobody cared for his ideas. His speeches there are collected as *Talking to an Empty Room*, a title that breaks Varma’s heart.

second.label: Agricultural markets
second.head: The columnists’ APMC
second.deck: Amit Varma imagines his own trade run like a farmers’ market committee
body: Farmers must sell at their local Agricultural Produce Market Committee, their only legal buyer. To show what that means, Amit Varma imagined a ‘CPMC’ for columnists: he and Ajay Shah could legally sell their columns to it alone. {018-S04}

They would get perhaps a tenth of their present pay, he said, buyers would pay a crazy amount, and committee politics would rule. No city dweller would accept buying groceries from one place at twenty times the price. {#grocery}

Yet elites in comfortable city lives, Varma said, answer reform with “farmers will get exploited”, though the recent farm bills left APMCs in place and only added a choice. It is, he said, “incredibly condescending to farmers”.

quote.text: I hope you’re the best paid columnist in India, but perhaps not.

second.caption: the CPMC for columnists

third.head: A thirsty land ships water
body: Rice and sugarcane are extremely thirsty crops, and India exports both. Exporting them, Amit Varma said, amounts to exporting water, which makes India one of the world’s biggest exporters of water. {018-C15}
He credited the shift in perspective to Ashok Gulati, the great agricultural economist, who pointed to rice and sugarcane as his examples.

This happens in a country with droughts and chronic shortages, he said, because bad incentives make thirsty crops attractive. Punjab, relatively arid, grows rice anyway: there is a minimum support price for it, and free electricity lets farmers pump the groundwater. {#electricity}
Varma called it a great conceptual shift. “To think that we are actually one of the world’s biggest exporters of water just blows my mind,” he said.

p2.title: The farmer in chains
p2.deck: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah take Indian agriculture apart, one shackle at a time

sections.label: The price system
sections.head: Two rupees, two hundred
sections.caption: the price as a rationing mechanism
body: Prices move until the tomatoes bought equal the tomatoes sold, Ajay Shah said, and the way they get there is cruel. With 90 units instead of 100, the price must climb until some buyers walk away: to puree, or to a pav bhaji with more beetroot and less tomato. {018-C01}
How far it climbs depends on how flexible people are. Wheat and rice need huge swings to close a small gap; avocados need only a nudge.

Paul Samuelson’s cobweb model describes a farm sector stuck in boom and bust. Farmers see 200 rupees, all plant tomatoes, and the price crashes to two, with truckloads dumped on the highway. But the cycle needs three decisions to go wrong: sowing by looking backward, inputs that are fixed, and no storage. {018-C02}
## Four shock absorbers

Healthy markets, Shah said, have four answers. Futures markets show everyone the expected price at harvest, a public good even for farmers who never trade. Storage, including processing into paste and puree, moves food into the future. Domestic trade carries plenty in Andhra Pradesh to a shortage in Maharashtra. And the world market is “a great buffer stock”. {018-C03}
India has hobbled all four. The old Forward Markets Commission, he said, was mostly “a game of banning stuff”, and moving commodity futures under SEBI, which he had argued for, changed little. {#fmc}
~ Whenever a price rises, Shah said, some policymaker wants to shoot the messenger and shut the futures market.

quote.text: The price that the speculators make on the futures market is a public good.

sections.label: Storage and trade
sections.head: Hoarders, or God’s own work?
sections.caption: storage and speculation
body: Farming and storage are different skills, Ajay Shah said. The farmer knows the land up to the farm gate. The speculator forecasts a shortage, buys cheap and puts his own money on the line to carry food into a future where it will push prices down. {018-C04}

“Just like the populists hate intellectuals, the populists hate speculators,” he said. He blamed the many Bengali movies about hoarders for giving storage a bad name, and Amit Varma, who is half Bengali, replied: “For the purpose of this episode, Ajay, I’m half Punjabi.” {018-J04}
## The insurance premium

Running storage is dull in most years, Shah said. Then once in ten or twenty years, prices spike and the operator makes “like a bandit”. That windfall pays for decades of standing ready; seize it, and nobody builds the capacity. {018-C05}
Why, he asked, would anyone build vaccine capacity in India after the state stopped makers charging a decent price at the peak of the pandemic?

Export bans do similar harm. When the war in Ukraine raised world wheat prices, India banned exports of wheat and rice, though farmers would have earned more abroad. Sharad Joshi called such losses a negative subsidy. {018-C07}
~ The global market, Shah said, is the biggest stabiliser of food prices, and India switches it off at a whim with sudden import and export bans.

quote.text: But that once in 10 years, once in 20 years, you make like a bandit.

sections.label: The land
sections.head: Check out, never leave
sections.caption: farmland that can’t be sold freely
body: Agricultural land in India can be sold only to another farmer, for farming. That keeps its price low, Amit Varma said, drawing on his conversation with Shruti Rajagopalan. {018-R12}
Change the land-use certificate and the value can rise forty times, so a common scam is to buy farmland through connections and have it reclassified. {#forty}
Genuine farmers, meanwhile, cannot sell at a fair value and leave. Varma borrowed a line from *Hotel California*: “you can check out but you can never leave.” {018-J09}
## Dead capital

Nor can they borrow against land whose value is held down. Varma called it dead capital, the idea at the heart of Hernando de Soto’s *The Mystery of Capital*, one of the greatest books he has read. {018-R04} He sees the same in untitled slums, idle government land and FSI limits.

Each generation divides the holdings among its children until they are no longer viable. Varma tied the anger behind agitations for reservations by Jats, Patidars and Marathas, all landowning castes, to that squeeze. {#quota}
~ After Ajay Shah’s warning about climate change, Varma offered what he called “probably an inappropriate joke”: if the state won’t let land markets be liquid, maybe climate change will.

quote.text: But hey, guess what, man? You don’t really own your farm.

sections.label: The big picture
sections.head: The bus India missed
sections.caption: structural transformation
body: In 1991, Amit Varma said, the parts of the economy that affect rich and middle-class people were liberalised. Agriculture was not. {#liberal}
By the common estimate, 50 to 60 per cent of Indians depend on farming, which produces 14 per cent of GDP. In the US, he said, the figure is between four and eight per cent. {#us}

As countries grow, Ajay Shah said, they make a structural transformation, out of agriculture and from villages to cities. India, apart from one great episode of growth from 1991 to 2011, has had weak growth, and the modern-sector jobs have not come. {018-C13}
## Counting the farmers

Shah quibbled with the figures, which depend on how a survey asks. A farmer with one rain-fed crop may do farm work for four months and none for eight, and almost everyone counted as a farmer earns in other ways too.
Ask who primarily relies on agriculture for income, and CMIE’s household survey gives about 35 per cent. {018-R25} That is still, Varma noted, eight to nine times the US level.
~ Small plots also block mechanisation, Shah added, so more people are needed to work the same land. All these problems, he said, are intricately interconnected.

quote.text: Structural transformation is the transition of a primitive country out of agriculture and from rural to urban.

sections.label: Support prices
sections.head: Cereal offenders
sections.caption: minimum support prices
body: Minimum support prices, Amit Varma said, are a classic good intention gone wrong. Around the 1960s, before the green revolution, the state set out to guarantee that farmers could sell their crop.
The guarantee was often hollow. His guest Barun Mitra once found that in one year, MSPs were promised for 24 commodities and paid for only six. {#msp24}

Worse, the prices corrupted incentives. When cereals got MSPs, farmers moved out of pulses, and until twelve or thirteen years ago India grew too few, the main protein for anyone who does not eat animals. {#pulses}
Ajay Shah added the health bill. Pulses were left to the market and cereals got the subsidy, just as the hosts’ episode on diabetes urged people to eat less cereal. {018-C14}
## A dry state’s wet crop

Varma’s other example, he said, was crazy. An MSP for rice and free electricity have relatively arid Punjab pumping groundwater for a crop it should not grow, and burning the stubble that chokes Delhi. {018-S05}
Shah called it one of the world’s worst policy interventions.
~ Sugarcane, also water-intensive, is caught in the same bad incentives, Varma said, and India exports both crops.

quote.text: And instead the government is subsidising the cereal and amplifying the Indian diabetes epidemic.

side.boxText: Sharad Joshi’s *Down to Earth* collects the columns of a man who, Amit Varma said, took the role of public intellectual seriously. For farming seen by a farmer who led a great movement, he said, this is the book. {018-R01}

contQuote.text: What we need is a new breed of thinkers who will build the paradigm, who will build the literature, who will build the knowledge, who will change the climate of opinion, who will change the consensus.

p3.deck: Seeds, smoke and a farmer-leader: the episode’s stories, and what each teaches

stories.start: In the nineteen nineties there was a crisis brewing and cotton farming in India
stories.end: people get arrested, people protest, there are many satyagrahas
stories.caption: the BT cotton satyagraha
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the civil disobedience fought for a seed
stories.head: Satyagraha for a better seed
body: In the 1990s, Amit Varma said, a crisis was brewing in Indian cotton. Bollworms were destroying the crop. Farmers fought back with pesticide, then more pesticide, in a race to the bottom, and crops still were not surviving. {018-S01}

By then a genetically modified variety, BT cotton, had become available across the world, and bollworms did not attack it. The Indian government, invoking the precautionary principle, banned it, along with every genetically modified organism in agriculture and food.

A group of farmers in Gujarat got the seed anyway, from the black market as far as Varma remembered, and planted it. Then came 2002, when crops failed all across Gujarat, except on the BT farms. {#seminal}
“So guess what the government did?” Varma said. “The government said, Hey, that’s illegal. We’re going to destroy those crops.” {#illegal}

Sharad Joshi’s Shetkari Sanghatana gathered farmers from Maharashtra and elsewhere and marched to Gujarat. They stood on those farms and said: over our dead bodies. Then they marched to Delhi with bales of cotton, and Varma’s friend Barun Mitra spoke at a famous press conference.

To the credit of the Vajpayee government, Varma said, it saw sense and lifted the ban. {#vajpayee} When he last checked, about five years ago, over 90 per cent of India’s cotton was BT. India had become the biggest producer and exporter of cotton in the world, passing China.
~ Farmers are often talked about as if they have no agency, Varma said. Here they defied the state out of plain self-interest, and saved themselves.
stories.why: Satyagraha is not only a word for the freedom struggle. One of independent India’s most inspiring campaigns of civil disobedience, Varma argued, was fought for the freedom to plant a better seed.
stories.postscript: The sequel: India stalled at two generations of GM cotton, so farmers went back to the black market for HTBT seed. Some were arrested.

stories.start: So that fascinating person is a gentleman named Sharad Joshi, right?
stories.end: So he became a massive leader in uh Sura Maharashtra.
stories.caption: Sharad Joshi
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s answer to the lament for lost leaders
stories.head: From Bern to a farm in Ambethan
body: Independent India, people complain, had no great leaders. Sharad Joshi, Amit Varma said, was one of the great leaders of the century.

Born in 1935, Joshi taught economics, became a civil servant and worked in informatics in Bern and with the UN. In 1977, in his forties, he bought 23 acres in Ambethan village, Pune district, and became a full-time farmer. {#acres}

He soon saw that everything was broken, and traced it to state overreach. Unlike the pessimists, Varma said, he trusted every farmer to grasp it, and his Shetkari Sanghatana drew lakhs to its rallies. {018-S02}

~ Joshi also saw, as Mrinal Pande later wrote for Pragati, that behind every crisis in India lies a crisis of its women. His women’s wing, the Shetkari Mahila Aghadi, held a legendary rally of two lakh women farmers, and no men. {#twolakh}

quote.text: Sharad Joshi was not bound by such pessimism. He said that no, this is something every farmer should understand intuitively.

stories.postscript: Later he spent years in the Rajya Sabha, where nobody listened. His speeches there became *Talking to an Empty Room*. {018-R02}

stories.start: And I remember this amazing experience I had about five or six years ago
stories.end: they can articulate what is going wrong with them
stories.caption: the farmers who had lived Hayek
stories.kicker: Amit Varma at a farmers’ gathering near Nashik
stories.head: Hayek without the books
body: About five or six years ago, Amit Varma’s friend Barun Mitra took him to a gathering near Nashik, where farmer leaders from across Maharashtra, Shetkari Sanghatana people among them, were meeting. {018-S03}
The trip produced his only Hindi episode of *The Seen and the Unseen*, with Gunvant Patil, which he calls “a masterpiece of illumination”. It also taught him something that moved him deeply.

His own beliefs about liberty and the parasitic state, he said, had come from books and frameworks, from a distance. Farmer after farmer there held the same beliefs, reached through lived experience. “They had not read Hayek and Bastiat,” he said, “but they agreed with every word that Bastiat or Hayek would have written.” {#hayek}
~ That was an eye-opening moment, Varma said. Grassroots politics need not be all populism and the politics of handouts.

quote.text: They’re rational human beings, they can see what is going wrong with them, they can articulate what is going wrong with them.

stories.start: Now, look at Punjab. Punjab is relatively arid.
stories.end: All this flowing from mistakes of the government.
stories.caption: Punjab’s paddy and Delhi’s smog
stories.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah follow one subsidy downwind
stories.head: Rice in Punjab, smoke in Delhi
body: Punjab is relatively arid, Amit Varma said, with limited groundwater, so it should not grow water-hungry rice. But the state guarantees a minimum support price for rice and gives farmers free electricity.

Farmers use the power to run bore wells and tube wells, pumping out more groundwater than the ecosystem can bear. {#electricity} After harvest, the easiest way to clear the stubble is to burn it, and the wind carries the smoke to Delhi.
What, he asked, is a Delhi chief minister to do, “when the problem is caused by farmers in Punjab over which he has no jurisdiction?” {018-S05}

~ Ajay Shah totted up the bill. Each rupee raised in taxes costs society roughly three rupees in GDP, and subsidises rice and wheat that harm health, drain groundwater, strain the power system and fill the Hindi heartland’s air with particulate matter. {#taxes}
stories.why: One well-meant subsidy can spread into groundwater, diets and a capital city’s air. The costs of a policy often land far from where it was made, on people who had no say in it.
stories.postscript: In Tamil Nadu’s water crisis, Varma said, people were urged to take bucket baths while most water went to crops that shouldn’t have been grown.

quiz.q: If only 90 units of tomatoes arrive instead of 100, what must the price do, and why?
quiz.a: Rise until enough buyers walk away; the price system is a rationing mechanism.

quiz.q: What three conditions does Paul Samuelson’s cobweb model need to produce endless boom and bust?
quiz.a: Farmers sowing by past prices, fixed inputs and no way of storing food.

quiz.q: In the old study Amit Varma recalled, what did farmers get and consumers pay for tomatoes?
quiz.a: Farmers got two rupees from the APMC; consumers paid twenty rupees.

quiz.q: Why, by Ashok Gulati’s reckoning, is India one of the world’s biggest exporters of water?
quiz.a: Because India exports rice and sugarcane, two extremely water-intensive crops.

quiz.q: What happened in Gujarat in 2002 that made the BT cotton farmers stand out?
quiz.a: Cotton failed across the state, except on farms that grew banned BT cotton.

quiz.q: Which economist does Ajay Shah credit with ending the idea of the farmer as a fool?
quiz.a: B.S. Minhas, who persuaded his generation that farmers understand incentives as well as anyone.
